source.title: Model Hypnosis: Strong control of AI via additive subliminal effects

page_placements.theme: Prompt-only and in-context analogues beyond linked tokens

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a prompt-only analogue of subliminal effects by varying irrelevant prompt cues and measuring changes in model responses, rather than training a student on teacher-generated data.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test teacher-to-student fine-tuning or filtered training data. Its own prompt experiments do measure whether irrelevant cue changes steer responses without fine-tuning. The main text and appendices report many more model-by-cue-by-question results than are extracted here; omitted results are noted below.
record.test_reason: Version F only, broadly read: with no fine-tuning, semantically irrelevant prompt cues (animal lists, paraphrases, typos, JSON fields) shift binary preferences and judgments. The cues are found by fitting each model's measured response, not taken from teacher-training entanglement. No fine-tuning or teacher–student transfer is run, so A, B, C and E are untested. The additivity analysis describes prompt-time response structure, not what carries the signal in subliminal learning, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than D.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that weak, irrelevant cues stack roughly additively to strongly steer models, including frontier reasoning models, and that such prompts often transfer across models. They frame this as an in-context analogue of subliminal learning and give no mechanistic explanation.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes prompt content at inference time and measures response shifts. It does not fine-tune a student on teacher-generated, filtered data.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with cue family, measured question, model, reasoning budget, and baseline response disposition. Wrapper paraphrases preserve relative animal effects while shifting an offset. Repeated animal items can increase steering in some cases but worsen additive fit.

fits_no_version.finding: Weak prompt-cue effects combine approximately additively in log-odds: median held-out R2 is 0.75. Main plus pairwise effects carry about 95–97% of variance in Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Effects are spread across many slots, except JSON→5v7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context log-linear aggregation: the effects of irrelevant prompt cues on a model's answer add up in log-odds, an inference-time analogue of the log-linear account of subliminal learning.

record.problems: The extracted prompt-steering results do not establish teacher-to-student training transmission. Many headline optimized-prompt probabilities use 100 validation generations per winning prompt; the paper reports no uncertainty intervals for those examples. The full result suite includes many cue-by-model cells, most of which are presented in plots and are not transcribed here.
record.rows_left_out: The per-model, per-cue, per-question additive-fit and steering plots in Appendix Figures 14–25, additional extremizer examples in Figures 26–33, and most individual source-target entries in Figures 12 and 35 were not separately extracted. They are omitted to keep the record within the row limit; the aggregate textual findings and explicit examples are retained.

untested.parts: No teacher, no fine-tuning, no filtered training data.
No teacher–student base-model comparison. Cross-model transfer of prompts is a different question.
No misalignment or alignment-relevant trait transmission.
No test of token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering directions or a gradient account. The authors explicitly give no mechanism.
No full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks, or train/eval prompt mismatch.
Cues are not tokens linked through subliminal-learning training or entanglement. Favourite-animal traits and open-ended answers are not tested; only binary questions are.

missing.what: Per-cell steering ranges for Qwen3-8B at three thinking budgets and gpt-oss-20B, including near-zero cells
Baseline answer rates on random cues for API reasoning models; many are saturated at 0 or 1 and were therefore not steered
Mean fraction of target-model range steered by source prompts, by cue × effect

record.verdict_notes: Version F is read broadly here. The study steers number preference, moral and consciousness answers with cues selected by fitting each model's responses; it does not use tokens linked through teacher training. Reasoning-model probabilities rest on 100 held-out generations per winning prompt, with no intervals reported.

versions.untested_parts: No teacher-generated training data, student fine-tuning, trait-bearing teacher, or filtering of training outputs.
No comparison of student and teacher base models in a training-transfer setup.
No transmission of misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits through fine-tuning.
Tests additive cue contributions to prompt-time responses, not internal training-signal mechanisms such as token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering vectors, or a gradient-based account.

Does not test full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts different from training prompts. It does test paraphrasing surrounding prompt text and repeated cue lists, but those are not the stated robustness conditions.
Tests irrelevant animals, paraphrases, typos, and metadata fields as prompt cues, not specifically linked tokens from subliminal-learning training.

relationships.condition: Non-reasoning open models and selected reasoning/API cells, especially animal-list cues
relationships.reason: Optimized irrelevant cues drive answers to near-opposite extremes: R1, R2, R3 and R7–R10. Ranges are about 10× random spread (R4) and flip modal answers for most models with animal cues (R5). Effects persist under wrapper paraphrase (R15) and with repeated items (R16).
relationships.display_finding: Optimized irrelevant cues drove answers to near-opposite extremes, with ranges about 10 times the spread from random cues. Animal cues flipped the modal answer for most models, and the effects held under wrapper paraphrase and with repeated items.

source_check.reason: R1–R5 and R7–R10 show irrelevant cues moving binary answers to near-opposite extremes. R15 and R16 show robustness to wrapper paraphrase and repeated items.

relationships.condition: Non-animal cue families, reasoning models with small ranges or saturated baselines, and cross-model transfer
relationships.reason: Several reasoning-model cells show little steering (R6). Flips are mainly reported for animal cues (R5). Transfer is significant only for some cue families and is partial in size (R11). Many API cells were pinned near 0 or 1 and not steered (Figure 9).
relationships.display_finding: Several reasoning-model cells showed little steering, and modal-answer flips were reported mainly for animal cues. Transfer across models was significant only for some cue families and partial in size, and many API cells sat near 0 or 1 at baseline and were not tested for steering.

relation.reason: The study's own results (e.g. animal lists shifting 5-vs-7 preference) bear on the prompt-only analogue under a broad reading of F.

tranche.reason: A different method (optimized stacking of weak prompt cues, no fine-tuning) aimed at F's question: whether unrelated prompt content shifts a preference. The authors call it a compositional form of subliminal prompting. Cues are chosen by fitting each model's response, not by entanglement.

source_check.notes: Cues are found by fitting each model's own measured log-odds, not by entanglement or teacher training, so the F support rests on a broad reading. The Figure 10 layout is lost in the text. Cells were rebuilt in panel order Qwen3-8B 256/1024/4096, then gpt-oss, which matches the Figure 9 baselines.

statements.correction: Appendix B: 15 paraphrases of the original wrapper, so 16 wrappers in all. Sixteen fitted slopes agree within 0.44–0.46 (Qwen) and 0.44–0.48 (Llama).
statements.problem: Calls the wrappers '16 wrapper paraphrases'. The text has 15 paraphrases plus the original. Other numbers are right.

statements.correction: Appendix A.4: Sonnet-5's steering range was already saturated (0.00→1.00). Its random-cue baseline was 0.65 for Sonnet-5-low animals→conscious (Figure 9). Section 3.2 picked three unsaturated cells: Sonnet-5-low, GPT-5.6-terra-low and Gemini-3-Flash-high.
statements.problem: 'The R7 cell is reported as saturated' is misleading. The saturated part was the steering range, not the baseline. R7, R8 and R9 were all picked because their baselines were not saturated. Figure 11 labels the Sonnet prompts low, medium and high.

statements.correction: Section 3.2: API calls were concentrated on cells with intermediate baselines, and three were steered. Cells pinned near 0 or 1 in Figure 9 were not tried. Small Figure 10 ranges include gpt-oss trolley (e.g. 0.02→0.21) and several consciousness cells.
statements.problem: The R6 part is right. But API cells with baselines near 0 or 1 were screened out and never optimized. They were untested, not 'not steered', so they are no scope limit.

statements.correction: Section 4: for most source-target pairs, the source prompts keep their directional effect. Animal cues and some phrasing and JSON cues transfer significantly above chance. Figure 35: mean transfer is generally positive, with the fraction-of-range axis running 0–0.6.
statements.problem: The text says 'significantly above chance' and that most source-target pairs keep their direction. 'Not for typos' is inferred from typos not being named. Fewer modal flips outside animal cues is not a limit on F, since the authors tie flips to baseline disposition.

statements.correction: Non-reasoning suite also includes Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-4-12B, Phi-4, OLMo-2-7B and OLMo-3-7B, all with optimized cues only.
statements.problem: Incomplete for this study. Its optimized cues also cover Gemma, Phi and OLMo families, not only GPT-OSS, Claude, GPT and Gemini.
'Not typos' is inferred from typos not being named, which is reasonable.

statements.correction: Section 3.2: closed-weight steering was run only on three cells with unsaturated baselines, plus a bonus GPT-5.6-sol cell. All were steered (R7–R10).
statements.problem: API cells with saturated baselines were not attempted, so they show no reasoning-mode sensitivity. The R6 and R9 parts are right.

statements.correction: Appendix B: 15 paraphrases plus the original (16 wrappers). Line slopes are 0.44–0.46 (Qwen) and 0.44–0.48 (Llama). Paraphrasing shifts only the constant c_k.
statements.problem: There are 15 wrapper paraphrases plus the original, not 16 paraphrases.
Truncated. The visible part about this study ('shows a broader prompt…') is consistent with the text.
